sources.articleTitle: Australia delays final vote on gas reservation law for LNG exporters to February
Live: Gas reservation rubber-stamped in early morning sitting
Coalition teams up with Labor to pass 20% gas reservation scheme for Australia’s largest exporters

headline: Australian Parliament Passes Twenty Percent Gas Reservation Scheme
metaDescription: The Australian parliament has enacted a gas reservation scheme requiring major exporters to reserve 20% of their product for domestic supply.
aiSummaryBullets: The Australian federal government successfully passed a gas reservation policy requiring major exporters to keep 20% of their output for domestic use.
The legislation received bipartisan support in the Senate from both the Labor government and the Coalition opposition.
Parliament rejected an alternative proposal from the Greens party that aimed to impose a 25% tax on gas exports.
aiContextParagraph: Australia, currently ranked as the world's second-largest supplier of liquefied natural gas following disruptions related to the conflict involving Iran, has long exported a significantly higher volume of gas than it consumes domestically. To address domestic energy security, the federal government introduced a legislative framework aimed at ensuring a portion of natural gas production remains within the country. The final piece of major legislation for 2026 passed through the House of Representatives during an early morning sitting and gained formal approval in the Senate. While the government had initially faced reports of potential delays to early 2027, the policy proceeded with the support of the Coalition. The passage of this law represents a definitive shift in energy regulation, as lawmakers opted for the reservation quota over other proposed measures, such as the 25% export tax previously advocated by the Greens.
whyItIsViral: This legislative development is currently being reported by three independent media outlets and gained significant momentum following the final parliamentary session of the year.
